summary: Gives guidance to authors of specifications that were written with a now-deprecated version of ASN.1, since not all ASN.1 compilers support both old and current syntax. It is informational and relates to specifications in the Security Area.

eli5.summary: Some old documents use an older dialect of a data-description language, and some tools only understand the newer one. This explains how to translate between the dialects.

subtitle: Converting specifications between ASN.1 syntax versions without changing encoded data.

tldr.problem: Specifications written in the 1988 version of ASN.1 (X.208) and those using the 1998-2002 versions (X.680-X.683) use incompatible syntax, but not all ASN.1 compilers support both.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a systematic guide to translate ASN.1 modules from one version to another while ensuring the encoded data on the wire remains unchanged using Basic Encoding Rules (BER) or Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).
tldr.outcome: Specification authors and implementers can modernize legacy ASN.1 definitions or convert new definitions to older syntax as needed, ensuring compatibility with different compiler generations.

today: RFC 6025 is an Internet Standard (Informational). It remains the guidance for translating ASN.1 modules between the two syntax versions without changing encoded data.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) is widely used in the IETF Security Area to define the structure of data in security protocols, certificates, and cryptographic messages. The standard has two major versions: X.208 from 1988 and the series X.680-X.683 from 1998-2002 (referred to as X.68x). Not all ASN.1 compiler vendors have updated to support both versions, creating a practical problem for implementers.

This RFC addresses that problem by providing a translation guide for specification authors and implementers. The goal is to convert ASN.1 modules from one version to another without causing any changes to the encoded results when using BER (Basic Encoding Rules) or DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) for encoding.
sections.eli5: ASN.1 is like a recipe for packing data into bytes. The old and new recipes use different instructions, but the packed result should be identical. This document explains how to translate the recipe.

sections.title: The Two Versions of ASN.1
sections.content:
The 1988 version (X.208) was defined in a single ITU-T document. It uses simpler syntax and is the baseline version. The 1998-2002 versions (X.680-X.683) come as a series of four documents covering basic notation, information objects, constraints, and parameterization. For convenience, this RFC refers to the series collectively as X.68x.

X.68x is a superset of X.208 in functionality: everything that can be written in X.208 can be expressed in X.68x, but X.68x introduces new features that X.208 does not support. The two versions have different character sets and syntax rules, which creates the translation challenge.
sections.eli5: The old version is like simplified English; the new version is like full English with more options. Both can describe the same things, but the new one can say things the old one cannot.

sections.title: Key Design Differences
sections.content:
The main differences between X.208 and X.68x cluster into a few categories. Open types are the most significant: X.208 uses ANY DEFINED BY to associate data with a type identifier (usually an OBJECT IDENTIFIER), whereas X.68x provides Information Object Classes, which formalize this relationship so compilers can verify it. Both versions support using OCTET STRINGs or BIT STRINGs as containers for encoded data.

Constraints are another major difference. X.68x allows constraints on values using information objects (simple table constraints and component relation constraints), which X.208 cannot express. Parameterization lets X.68x define generic types with parameters, similar to macros in X.208. Versioning is managed differently: X.68x uses extension markers (ellipsis) and version brackets to mark extensibility and evolution, whereas X.208 has no formal mechanism.

The character set differs as well: X.68x adds characters such as exclamation mark, ampersand, asterisk, forward slash, semicolon, greater-than, at sign, caret, underscore, and pipe to the X.208 set.
sections.eli5: The new version has fancier ways to say what you mean. The old version uses comments and explanations in prose instead of formal syntax.

sections.title: Translation Approaches
sections.content:
Downgrading from X.68x to X.208 is mechanically straightforward because you are deleting features. The process involves removing all Information Object Class definitions, replacing fixed-type references with concrete types, deleting constraints and CONTAINING statements, replacing variable-type references with ANY or ANY DEFINED BY, removing version and extension markers, and manually resolving parameterized types. The constraints that are removed should be captured in prose or comments to preserve their intent.

Upgrading from X.208 to X.68x can range from minimal changes (replacing deprecated ANY DEFINED BY with Information Object Class references, adding extension markers) to comprehensive modernization (introducing formal Information Object Classes and constraints). A minimalist upgrade just eliminates deprecated syntax. A comprehensive upgrade defines object classes, constrains fields using object sets, and formalizes the relationship between identifiers and types, which gives compilers more power to validate and generate code.
sections.eli5: Going to the new syntax means adding structure. Going to the old syntax means removing features and replacing them with notes.

sections.title: Today and Security Notes
sections.content: This document is informational. When modules are downgraded from X.68x to X.208, constraints that were automatically enforced by the compiler are lost. These constraints must be re-expressed in prose or enforced by other means (such as manual validation in code). When modules are upgraded, the programmer is responsible for ensuring that any constraints expressed in prose are also enforced in the ASN.1 or in the generated code, depending on the compiler's capabilities.
sections.eli5: When you simplify the description, you lose some automatic checks. You need to make sure your program still checks everything that matters.
